title: The Night Sky: Constellations and Coordinates

cards.h: Your first map of the universe
cards.b:
Before telescopes, the sky was the only map, clock and calendar humans had. Farmers planted by it. Sailors steered by it.

Look up on a clear night far from city lights and you can see roughly 2,500 stars at a time. They look like dots on a dome. They are not. They sit at wildly different distances. This lesson gives you the language for finding your way around that dome.

A constellation is a pattern we imagine by joining bright stars. The stars in it are usually unrelated. One may be 40 light-years away, its neighbour 800.

Every culture drew its own pictures. In 1922-1930 the International Astronomical Union fixed 88 official constellations, each a patch of sky with firm borders, like countries on a map. Orion, Ursa Major (the Great Bear, with the Saptarishi 'Big Dipper') and Crux (the Southern Cross) are familiar ones.

Imagine all stars painted on a huge sphere around Earth. It is a useful fiction: we cannot feel depth in the sky, but we can measure directions exactly.

Extend Earth's axis outward and you get the north celestial pole. Extend the equator and you get the celestial equator. The whole sphere seems to turn once a day, but that is really Earth spinning the other way: 15 degrees every hour.

cards.h: Why the Pole Star stays put
cards.b:
Polaris lies within about 1 degree of the north celestial pole, so as Earth spins it hardly moves. Everything else circles it. In India it is Dhruva.

A neat trick: the height of Polaris above your horizon equals your latitude. At Delhi (28.6 N) it sits about 28 degrees up. At the equator it sits on the horizon. At the North Pole it is straight overhead. Navigators used this for centuries.

cards.h: Two ways to give a star an address
cards.b:
Horizon system: altitude (angle above horizon) and azimuth (compass direction). Easy, but it changes with place and time.

Equatorial system: fixed to the stars, like latitude and longitude. Declination is the north-south angle from the celestial equator. Right ascension is the east-west position, measured in hours (0 to 24) from the point where the Sun crosses the equator at the March equinox.

Because the address is fixed to the stars, a star keeps the same coordinates wherever you stand.

cards.h: The sky changes with the hour and the season
cards.b:
Through one night stars rise in the east and set in the west. Through the year, the same star rises about 4 minutes earlier each night, because Earth moves along its orbit. After a year the pattern returns.

This is why Orion rules winter evenings and Scorpius rules summer ones: in different seasons our night side faces different parts of space. Also, the pole slowly wobbles like a spinning top, called precession, taking about 26,000 years. Around 3000 BCE the pole star was Thuban; in about 12,000 years it will be Vega.

Positions were first measured with sighting rods, quadrants and later the telescope. Hipparchus (c. 130 BCE) made a star catalogue and noticed precession by comparing his data with older records. He also began the magnitude scale for brightness.

Today the ESA's Gaia satellite (launched 2013) has measured the positions of nearly two billion stars to a tiny fraction of a milli-arcsecond. Old records, new satellites: same method, sharper tools.

• 'Stars in a constellation are close.' No. They only line up from our viewpoint.
  • 'The Pole Star is the brightest star.' No. Polaris is only moderately bright. Sirius is the brightest in the night sky.
  • 'Astrology and astronomy are linked science.' The zodiac constellations are real star patterns, but no experiment has shown that star positions shape human lives.

Indian astronomers divided the Moon's path into 27 nakshatras (lunar mansions): about one for each night the Moon takes to cross the sky. They appear in the Vedic texts and are still used in the panchang.

The Saptarishi are the seven bright stars of Ursa Major. Their two end stars point toward Dhruva. Mriga (Orion) and Lubdhaka (Sirius) are named in Indian lore. Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II built the stone observatories called Jantar Mantar (Delhi 1724, Jaipur and others) to measure star and Sun positions with huge masonry instruments.

• Constellations are 88 official sky regions; their stars are not physically linked.
  • The celestial sphere is a model: poles and equator are Earth's extended outward.
  • Polaris' altitude equals your latitude.
  • Right ascension and declination fix a star's address.
  • Precession shifts the pole star over about 26,000 years.

Think about it: (1) Why would an observer in Chennai see stars that a person in Srinagar never sees? (2) If the Sun were removed, would the constellations visibly change within your lifetime? Why?

quiz.q: How many official constellations has the IAU defined?
Why can the stars in one constellation be very far apart in real distance?
o: The pattern is just a line of sight effect
quiz.w: We see only direction, not depth.

quiz.q: The height of Polaris above the northern horizon equals the observer's:
From Earth, the whole sky seems to turn once a day mainly because:
quiz.w: Rotation of Earth, 15 degrees per hour.

quiz.q: Declination on the sky is most like which Earth coordinate?
Why does a given star rise about 4 minutes earlier each night?
quiz.w: Earth's orbital motion shifts the sky by about 1 degree per day.

quiz.q: Precession of Earth's axis takes about:
Which is the brightest star in the night sky?
quiz.w: Sirius; Polaris is only moderately bright.

quiz.q: How many nakshatras are in the traditional Indian lunar mansion scheme?
Why is the equatorial coordinate system more useful for catalogues than altitude-azimuth?
o: A star's coordinates stay almost fixed for any observer
quiz.w: It is fixed to the stars, not to place and time.
